Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“How one becomes what one is.”
German
“Wie man wird, was man ist.”

The subtitle of Ecce Homo. The thought is older than the book — Nietzsche credits Pindar, whose second Pythian ode has “become such as you are, having learned what that is.”

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “Become what you are.”
  • “How one becomes what one is.”

Attribution notes

“Become what you are” usually reaches readers through Pindar or through the English title of the Ecce Homo subtitle, and it is then read as an encouragement to self-expression. In Nietzsche the phrase is about the long, unfree process by which a person's disparate drives are disciplined into a single style — the becoming is not willed, it is survived.

About Friedrich Nietzsche

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German classical philologist who became a radical critic of morality, metaphysics, and modern culture. Appointed professor at Basel at twenty-four, he resigned from ill health and wrote in solitude across Switzerland, Italy, and Germany.

How to read this passage

To ask about the self is to ask what persists through experience, what can be known from the first-person point of view, and how character is formed. Some traditions treat the self as a substantial soul; others as a stream of experience, a social role, or a practical center of agency. This passage enters that discussion through self.

What is the source of the quotation “How one becomes what one is.”?

“How one becomes what one is.” comes from Ecce Homo, (subtitle; from Pindar), attributed to Friedrich Nietzsche.

To ask about the self is to ask what persists through experience, what can be known from the first-person point of view, and how character is formed. Some traditions treat the self as a substantial soul; others as a stream of experience, a social role, or a practical center of agency. This passage enters that discussion through self.

Is the wording of this Friedrich Nietzsche quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “How one becomes what one is.” Forms in circulation that differ: Become what you are. / How one becomes what one is. The German reads “Wie man wird, was man ist.”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

In Nietzsche the phrase is about the long, unfree process by which a person's disparate drives are disciplined into a single style — the becoming is not willed, it is survived.
